## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}
There two entry points to think of a distribution.
The first one is from the theoretical perspective, thinking about normal/gaussian or like binomial or Poission distribution.
That perspective will be addressed later in this book, when we talk about statistical inference.

The second one is from a data-driven perspective.
Assume for now that it is qualitative variable (@sec-qualitative-variable).
That is, imagine assess the gender of all (n) employees in a company (more generally a variable @sec-variable from a population @sec-population).
That is mostly a sequence of male female.
A distribution is a first entry point to summarizing your data.
Yes, it is a summary because we are computing new numbers from the original data.
So what are the new numbers: essentially look at the unique types of variables and count how many are males and female. So you have a pair male- nmale and female-nfemale.
Ultimately, a distribution is a figure, the figure is simply two bars of different height.

You are most bored at this stage, this is so obvious...but what happens variable is quantitative (@sec-quantiative-variable)? How one constructs a distribution?
Imagine you measured the height of the employees, you have a sequence of n numbers. Because numbers are likel unique, one cannot count how many have the same value (plotting that would be the same height). The work around is to arbitrarily divide the range into intervals and count the number of (as above with male-female).
The key important word here is arbirarily because depending on the intervals, it is possible to create different distribution
Back in the day, Excel did not have a dedicated function to create a histogram, so one has to create the intervales, computes and then use bar chart to make to plot the distribution.
Now, it is done with a single click and the program default the interval.


The take-home is that a data is a sequence of number and the distribution transform it into pair of discrete bin-and the number of that fall belong to that bin which is then plotted for visualization (@sec-function_viz). You can then see which value is most or least frequent (maro an'isa or vitsy an'isa), but also the frequency of all other values.


## Formal {.unnumbered}

In statistics, a distribution (or the distribution of a variable) is a foundational concept that bridges raw data with mathematical probability. Depending on whether you look at an applied context (real data) or a theoretical context (probability models), it is defined either as a summary of observed frequencies or as a mathematical function mapping probabilities to values.
Here are the rigorous definitions from three authoritative textbooks representing these different levels of statistical analysis.

1. The Applied / Data-Centric Definition
In applied and introductory statistics, the distribution of a variable is defined as a description of what values the variable takes and how often it takes them.

Textbook Source
Book: The Practice of Statistics (6th Edition, 2018)
Authors: Daren S. Starnes and Josh Tabor
Publisher: W. H. Freeman / Bedford, Freeman & Worth

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Data Analysis"), Starnes and Tabor provide the standard, universally taught definition for the distribution of an observed variable:
"The distribution of a variable tells us what values the variable takes and how often it takes these values. The distribution of a categorical variable lists the categories and gives either the count or the percent of individuals who fall in each category. The distribution of a quantitative variable tells us what values the variable takes and how often it takes those values."

2. The Rigorous Mathematical Statistics Definition
In theoretical statistics, when we talk about the distribution of a variable, we are referring to a Probability Distribution, which is formalized as a function (like a Cumulative Distribution Function, or CDF).

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), the authors define the distribution of a random variable X by its cumulative distribution function FX(x), which rigorously maps out the entire probability behavior of that variable:
"Let X be a random variable. The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of X, denoted by FX(x), is defined by

FX (x)=P(X≤x)

for all real numbers x. [...] The cdf completely determines the probability distribution of the random variable X."


Under this mathematical framework:

If the variable is discrete, its distribution is rigorously defined by a Probability Mass Function (PMF): p(x)=P(X=x).

If the variable is continuous, its distribution is rigorously defined by a Probability Density Function (PDF), f(x), such that P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab f(x)dx.

3. The Measure-Theoretic Definition
For advanced graduate-level mathematical statistics, a distribution is rigorously defined as a "probability measure" induced by the variable on a measurable space.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics (2nd Edition, 2003)
Author: Jun Shao
Publisher: Springer Science & Business Media

The Definition
In Chapter 1, Shao strips away the informal language entirely, defining the distribution of a variable (X) as a mathematically bound probability law:

"Let X be a random variable defined on a probability space (Ω,F,P). The distribution of X is defined as the probability measure P
X on (R,B) induced by X, i.e.,

P X (B)=P(X−1(B)) = P({ω∈Ω:X(ω)∈B}) for any Borel set B∈B."

Summary: What does a "Distribution" encompass?
No matter the tier of the textbook, a distribution must provide two essential components for a variable:

The Values: Every possible value (or range of values) that the variable can mathematically achieve.

The Frequency/Probability: The likelihood, proportion, or exact frequency with which those values occur.

Visually and analytically, we evaluate the distribution of a variable by looking at its shape (e.g., symmetric, skewed, bell-shaped), its center (e.g., mean, median), and its spread (e.g., variance, standard deviation).


## Examples {.unnumbered}
We show figures here but the figures are obtained from numbers.

Qualitative
```{r}
df_sex <- data.frame(
    sex = c("male", "female"),
    value = c(13, 16)
)

fig_sex <- ggplot(df_sex, aes(x = sex, y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()

df_lemur <- data.frame(
    species = c("indri", "catta", "mouse"),
    value = c(10, 20, 300)
)

fig_lemur_a <- ggplot(df_lemur, aes(x = species, y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()

fig_lemur_b <- ggplot(df_lemur, aes(x = reorder(species, value), y = value)) +
    geom_col() +
    theme_bw()


fig_qual <- fig_sex + fig_lemur_a + fig_lemur_b +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")

fig_qual
```

Quantitative
```{r}

# Quantitative
set.seed(1)
df_discrete <- data.frame(
    size = rpois(100, 5)) |>
    count(size)


fig_discrete <- ggplot(df_discrete, aes(x = size, xend = size, y = 0, yend = n)) +
 geom_point(aes(x = size, y = n)) +
  geom_segment() +
  theme_bw()

set.seed(1)
df_quant <- data.frame(
    size = rnorm(100, 10, 1)
)

fig_quant_a <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant_b <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant <- fig_discrete + fig_quant_a + fig_quant_b +
    plot_layout(axis_titles = "collect")
fig_quant
```

```{r}
fig_quant_dens <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size, after_stat(density))) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_quant_freq <- ggplot(df_quant, aes(x = size, after_stat(ncount))) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
    theme_bw()

fig_y <- fig_quant_a + fig_quant_dens + fig_quant_freq
fig_y
```


Play with y






## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
It could be anything but we are so used to theoretical distribution.
Continuous is unintuitive.


As a final point, the height can be scaled (e.g. total number of individuals or the frequency as a percentage with sums to 100 or a proportion which sums to 1)

Difference between bar chart and histogram.

A figure is worth a thousand words
